PAPER
Bio-inspired minimal hardware implementation of spike-time
dependent plasticity for intelligent spiking neural networks
Adrien d’Hollande1, Olivier Schneegans 2, Kang W ang1 and Marcelo Rozenberg3,4,∗
1 Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS Laboratoire de Physique des Solides, 91405 Orsay, France
2 Group of Electrical Engineering of Paris (GeePs), CentraleSupélec, CNRS, Paris-Saclay and Sorbonne Universities, 91192 Gif-sur-
Yvette, France
3 Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center, Paris 75006, France
4 Department of Physics, University of California, San Diego, CA 92093, United States of America
∗ Author to whom any correspondence should be addressed.
E-mail: marcelo.rozenberg@cnrs.fr
Keywords: neuromorphic hardware, spiking neural networks, spike-timing dependent plasticity
Abstract
W e introduce a hardware circuit model that implements spike-time dependent plasticity (STDP)
to endow spiking neural networks with learning capabilities. Our circuit model is characterized as
both minimal and bio-inspired, due to its simplicity and to a novel active dendrite compartment
that mimics the synaptic potentiation mechanism. The active dendrite consists of an integrate-
and-fire stage which produces a train of pulses whose number is inversely related to the timing
between pre- and post-synaptic spikes. The dendrite pulses modulate in a reliable manner the
synaptic efficacy (conductance) that we implemented with a digipot, considered as an idealized
non-volatile memristor. W e demonstrate the behavior of the circuit by implementing a minimal
spiking neuron model of associative learning by STDP , which is analog to the classic conditioning
experiment of Pavlov’s dog.
1.Introduction
Understanding learning is one of the greatest open challenges in science and is key to endow intelli-
gence to systems and devices. Contributions to this problem are multidisciplinary, originating in fields
that range from neuroscience to computer science, psychology, and more. The mechanistic origin of
learning, at the level of neuronal circuits, is based on the widely accepted dogma that it is rooted in the
modification of synaptic efficacies due to experience. The evolution of the synaptic strengths between
neurons tailors the architecture of neural networks and enables animals and humans to acquire new
motor and cognitive functions. While this topic is a matter of intense research, a main paradigm for
the modification of synaptic couplings is the experimentally observed spike-timing dependent plasticity
(STDP) [ 1–3]. This mechanism is often viewed as Hebb’s famous statement ‘cells that fire together wire
together’ [ 4].
STDP can be considered as the natural mechanism for a pair of neurons to build-up correlations
between their spiking activities. In the celebrated Pavlov’s dog experiment [ 5], an initially neutral stim-
ulus, such as the ringing of a bell, is presented along an unconditioned one, such as food. After a few
‘teaching’ sessions where the two stimuli are presented together, the dog learns that a bell is associated
with food, and starts drooling at the sole ringing. Hence a correlation has formed between two previ-
ously unrelated phenomena: the neural response to the sound of a bell and the neural stimulation of a
saliva producing gland.
That celebrated experiment is an example of supervised learning, as it requires the action of a
‘teacher’ . Nevertheless, the STDP mechanism is also associated to a more challenging type of learning,
called unsupervised. In this case, an animal, or a neural network, learns from its own experience, that is,
by trial an error. In that case the neural correlations are built as consequence of a self-produced mech-
anism such as pleasure or dislike. This should not be confused with an innate behavior, which may be
© 2026 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd
Neuromorph. Comput. Eng.6 (2026) 034015 A d’Hollande et al
Figure1. T op: schematic of a pre and post synaptic neurons i and j. The coupling between them is characterized by the efficacy
Wij. Bottom: schematics of typical STDP functional forms. Left: antisymmetric STDP promotes the build-up of causal correla-
tions (∆τ > 0), and depresses the synaptic efficacy upon anti-causal spike events. Right: potentiation of correlations for firing in
coincidence, regardless of causality. The time-scale τp is the synaptic plasticity time.
due to a pre-wiring of the network. Typical examples of unsupervised behavior are classification tasks.
For instance, discovering tasty fruits or clustering in the classroom, such as when children go about dis-
tinguishing friends from foes in pre-school.
The STDP mechanism can be mathematically formalized by defining the change in the synaptic effi-
cacy ∆W as a function to the relative timing ∆τ between the spike emission events of the two neurons
sharing that synapse. Concretely, let ∆τij denote the time difference tj − ti between spikes fired by the
pre-synaptic neuron i and the post-synaptic neuron j, coupled by the synaptic efficacy Wij (see figure 1).
The type of STDP is characterized by the function ∆Wij(∆τij). Typically, this function is peaked at
small values of the argument, as it enhances correlations between the firing events of two neurons. If
the change ∆W is positive, it is called potentiation, as the coupling is made stronger. In contrast, if it is
negative, it is called depression, as the influence of one neuron on the other is decreased. For instance, if
the pre-neuron fires shortly before the post-neuron and ∆W is large and positive, then the STDP mech-
anism contributes to build-up a positive correlation between the firing of i and j, i.e. enhances a causal
relation between them. Figure 1 shows two common instances of STDP , and this can be generalized in
multiple ways [ 6].
The biological underpinning of the STDP mechanism is still a matter of study [ 7]. For the potentia-
tion of a synapse, one may argue that as a pre-synaptic action potential arrives to the synapse, it produce
a temporary sensitization of the junction during a plasticity time-scale τp. Then, if a post-synaptic action
potential occurs within the τp window, it may produce a spike signal that propagates upstream along
the post-synaptic dendrite. This back propagating potential may eventually hit the still sensitized synap-
tic junction and induce an increase in its efficacy. Motivated by such a process, in this work we shall
propose a phenomenological bio-inspired model for STDP that we implement in a minimal hardware
circuit. T o that end we shall adopt a recently introduced minimal hardware model of an excitable (i.e.
spiking) system [ 8, 9].
2.Model
2.1.BasicSTDPcircuit
W e shall first describe a rather schematic circuit implementation of STDP , which has some common fea-
tures found in many related previous work [ 10–15]. This basic circuit will serve us as a reference to later
introduce our novel bio-inspired hardware model. In a typical implementation of STDP , as shown in the
circuit of figure 2, and the schematic diagram in panel a of figure 3, the arrival of a pre-synaptic spike
Vpre creates a voltage trace Vp that decays within a characteristic plasticity time τp ≈ RpCp. This trace
enables the transistor M2 during τp, so long Vp ⪆ 0.7V , the threshold for polarization of M2. If a post-
synaptic spike Vpost arrives, it will generate a similar trace that enables the second transistor M1 during
a τp. If the time difference ∆τ between these two arrivals is smaller than τp, then both M1 and M2 will
be simultaneously enabled during a certain overlap time δt ∼ (τp − ∆τ ) > 0. During that time window
δt, a current ∆Ipot ≈ (Vpost − 0.7V)/Rpot will flow out of the current mirror CM. Hence, an amount of
2

Figure2. (a) Schematic of a basic STDP circuit. The upper part implements the potentiation (causal) case and the lower part the
depression (anti-causal) case. The (trans-) conductance GW represents the synaptic efficacy, which is controlled by the potential
of the capacitor CW. (b) Measured changes of the trans-conductance ∆G for three different values of τp = 3, 6.2 and 10 ms.
These were obtained for Cp = 10 nF and Rp = 300 kΩ (blue), 620 kΩ (greeen), 1 MΩ (yellow), respectively. Notice that ∆G
remains approximately constant at low ∆τ and then abruptly goes to zero as ∆τ ≈ τp.
Figure3. Timing to Pulse Number Conversion. Panela: arrival of pre- and post-spikes with timing difference ∆τ create respec-
tive traces of timescale τp. The overlap (orange region) is δt ≈ τp − ∆τ . Panelb: there is a current ∆I injected to the active den-
drite during the overlap time δt. This current drive the integrate-and-fire sub-circuit of the ADC producing a number of pulses n
proportional to δt.
charge δq ≈ ∆Ipotδt will be added to the weight capacitor CW, increasing the (trans-)conductance GW
in a certain ∆G which corresponds to the ∆W of figure 4. The conductance GW represent the synaptic
coupling and its increase provides a potentiation of its efficacy. Note that the amount ∆G is controlled
by the magnitude of the resistors Rpot (and Rdep for depression), as shown in figure 2.
A similar analysis can be done for the synaptic depression case that corresponds to the anti-causal
arrival of spikes. This is, when the pre-synaptic spike arrives after the post-synaptic one. The sole circuit
difference is the configuration of the current mirror that produces a negative ∆I. Therefore there is a
discharge of CW and a decrease of the synaptic conductance GW by a certain −∆G, whose value can be
controlled with Rdep.
The circuit just described was implemented and measured, and the behavior for three different values
of τp is shown in figure 2. W e observe that, consistent with the previous discussion, ∆G(∆τ ) shows a
dependence on the time-scale τp. However, one may consider a shortcoming of this simple STDP imple-
mentation that ∆G does not show a significant dependence on ∆τ , as it exhibits a step-like behavior.
3
Neuromorph. Comput. Eng.6 (2026) 034015 A d’Hollande et al
Figure4. Schematic of the bio-inspired STDP implementation.
This is unlike typical theoretical models of STDP which show a decaying behavior (cf figure 1). Another
shortcoming, perhaps more important, is rather practical as it is difficult to maintain the charge of CW
beyond the order of the second, due to its intrinsic leak. As we shall see below, these shortcomings will
be significantly improved by our bio-inspired STDP model circuit.
2.2.Bio-inspiredcircuitwithactivedendritecompartment(ADC)
Our new implementation is schematically shown in figure 4. It introduces two main features with
respect to the basic STDP model. Firstly, we replace the capacitor-plus-transistor that model the tun-
able synaptic conductance. Such a combination is hard to control due to both, the threshold behavior of
the transistor and the leak of CW. As we mentioned, the later is specially problematic, as it quickly erases
the eventual learning (although it may find applications in short term memory). Our practical solution
is to replace the capacitor plus transistor by a digital potentiometer (digipot). The digipot resistance (and
conductance) can be easily changed, up- or downwards, between 0 to Rmax in a number N of equal dis-
crete steps δr, such that Rmax = Nδr. It is interesting to mention that a digipot can also be considered
an idealized non-volatile memristor, i.e. a resistive component whose value can be tuned by application
of pulses [ 16]. Memristive materials and devices are under intense current research for energy-efficient
artificial intelligence hardware [ 17–19]. Our digipot solution has the merits of wide availability, reliability
and simple implementation. It therefore serves our present goal of introducing a novel STDP synaptic
circuit model. Nevertheless, the digipot component may eventually be replaced by non-volatile mem-
ristors, if low-energy and small footprint are required. The second and most important feature that we
introduce in our model is an active dendrite compartment (ADC, not to be confused with analog-digital
converter). This is a bio-inspired mechanism that allows to modify the synaptic weight depending on
the timing difference ∆τ . The ADC is modeled as an excitable sub-circuit that sends an upstream spik-
ing signal. T o implement these dendritic pulses W e adopt an integrate-and-fire circuit model based on
a volatile memristor device made of a thyristor-plus-resistor, which was recently introduced [ 8, 9]. The
ADC translates the delay ∆τ into a number of spikes that are used to modify the conductance value
of the synaptic digipot. As we shall see, an important feature of our circuit model is that, consistent
with theoretical STDP models and its experimental observation, the smaller the ∆τ , the stronger the
‘upstream’ signal and the larger the conductance change of the synapse. This bio-mimetic feature is
rarely implemented in hardware models. Our bio-inspired STDP circuit model is shown in figure 5.
Similarly to the basic circuit that we described before, this circuit also has two RC pairs at the input
to provide the two traces Vp
pre(t) and Vp
post(t) of the arriving spikes. As before, the traces start at the
arrival time of the spikes, tpre and tpost, and both decay exponentially with the time-constant τp ≈ RpCp
as shown in panel a of figure 3.
The pre- and post- traces, as in the previous circuit, enable the gates of two respective transistors
that are in series. When the traces overlap and they are simultaneously above 0.7V , the input side of the
current mirror is enabled. In this case, there is a current ∆I ≈ V+/Radc that flows during the overlap
time δt, as shown in panel b of figure 3. The current mirror reproduces the current ∆I at its output.
Hence, the ADC compartment gets as input the same current ∆I during a time δt. The ADC is mod-
eled as an excitable integrate-and-fire unit, similar as that introduced in [ 8]. Thus, the input ∆I to the
ADC produces a train of equally spaced spikes during the period δt, whose frequency is controlled by
the intensity of ∆I (i.e. integrate-and-fire model). Hence, the number n of spikes in the train is n ∝ δt.
Those spikes are subsequently reshaped into 0–5 V pulses by the two transistors as shown in figure 5
[8, 20], for proper input to the digipot. An example of this is displayed in figure 6: the first and second

difference ∆τ between the arrival of the pre- and post-synaptic spike, consistent with our previous dis-
cussion. When ∆τ ⪆ τp there are no more output spikes, where τp is the plasticity timescale. Since, as
noted before, δt ≈ τp − ∆τ the approximate behavior of the number of pulses in the train is

Lets now estimate the expected change in the STDP conductance ∆GW that this implementation
should provide. The digipot is characterized by its constant resistive change step δr. Hence, for a digipot
at an arbitrary initial resistance state RW, an incoming train of n pulses changes RW in a simple linear
fashion, i.e. ∆RW = ∓nδr (provided the final resistance RW + ∆RW does not reach any of the digipot
limits). The negative sign is for causal arrival, i.e. the pre-spike arrives before the post-spike, and the
plus of the anti-causal. This behavior is shown in the measured data of RW (in purple) in figure 6, for
both cases, causal and anti-causal.

causal STDP . Note that the dependence is well captured by the equation (5) and the behavior reflects the STDP timescale set by
τp = RpCp = 3.5 ms (cf figure 5).

initial state GW = 1/RW. W e have,

therefore, the change in the STDP conductance is also approximately linear in n, so long the initial value
of RW is not close to the low resistance end. In other words, it is much larger than the resistance step,
i.e. the initial RW ≫ δr. This condition can always be fulfilled by adding a small fixed series resistor to
RW, bigger than the resistive step.
W e should also note, from equation ( 4), that the change ∆GW has a non-linear dependence in the
initial value of GW = 1/RW. Specifically, given a number n of pulses in the train, the corresponding
∆GW will be relatively larger, the larger the initial value of GW. Within a learning scheme this qualita-
tively means that the initial learning stages (from low values of GW) are relatively ‘harder’ than the later
ones.
Using equation ( 1), we can finally estimate the change ∆GW(∆τ ). W e have,

which is a linearly decreasing function of ∆τ , in good agreement with the measured data shown in
figure 7, and qualitatively similar to the behavior depicted in figure 1.
W e need to discuss one more feature of the model circuit of figure 5, namely the RS flip-flop that
allows to keep the information of the order of arrival of the pre- and post-synaptic spikes. This sub-
circuit is optional. If it is not included, the STDP model provides a realization of the, ‘non-causal’ , sec-
ond type of function ∆W(∆τ ), as shown in figures 1 and 7. In this case, the arrival order, i.e. causal-
ity, is not important, Thus, the ( ±) drops out from the expressions above and ∆G(∆τ ) > 0 always
increases.
On the other hand, if causality is deemed important, the sub-circuit allows to toggle the digipot
between its up/down mode. W e implement this with a SR flip-flop that works as follows: assume the
initial inputs and output are all 0 and first consider a causal sequence. A logic 1 ( Vpre = 5V) arrives
at S (set), then the output Q changes to 1. A successive logic 1 arrives to R (reset), then the output Q
changes to 0. Hence, the digipot receives a logic 0 and goes to the down mode, ready to decrease its
resistance (cf fourth row of top panels in figure 6) when the spike train of the active dendrite arrives
(cf third row panels in figure 6). The output Q = 0 is maintained so long the R and S do not receive
spikes. In the anti-causal case, i.e. pre arrives after post, a 1 is received first at R and then at S. The out-
put Q of the flip-flop goes to 1 and it remains, so long no further pulses arrive. This sets the digipot to
the up mode. The increase of resistance for the anti-causal case can be observed in the fourth row of the
bottom panels of figure 6. W e implemented the SR flip-flop using two NOR gates.
One other feature that we should also mention about the circuit relates to an important bio-inspired
feature, the ‘dopamine effect’ , which is key for reinforcement learning. Dopamine is a neurotransmit-
ter that modulates the intensity of the synaptic changes. This is captured by our circuit in the follow-
ing manner: The intensity of the current ∆I controls the frequency of the pulses generated by the ADC.
6
Neuromorph. Comput. Eng.6 (2026) 034015 A d’Hollande et al
Hence, given a time-delay between the pre- and post- pulses, the magnitude of ∆I controls how many
pulses will be produced, ie the size of the STDP synaptic conductance change. The key point is that the
intensity of the current is controlled by the resistance Radc, as was described before. Therefore, the mag-
nitude of the conductance 1/Radc can be qualitatively assimilated to the effect of dopamine concentra-
tion, as it modulates the strength of the synaptic change. This feature may be exploited in implementa-
tions of networks with reinforcement learning by replacing Radc by a tunable resistance (such as a second
digipot or a non-volatile memristor).
3.Measuredcircuitbehavior
W e now illustrate the operation of the STDP with two different paradigmatic examples.
3.1.Synapticstrengthmodulation
In the first case we input two spike trains pre- and post- with a slightly different frequency. This pro-
duces a beating effect, namely the pre-spike precedes the post-spike during some time (causal ∆τ > 0)
and then the situation alternates and the post-spike precedes the pre-spike (anti-causal ∆τ < 0). Hence,
the change in the synaptic resistance (or conductance) periodically increases and decreases. This can be
seen in figure 8, which demonstrates the phenomenon and allows to appreciate the stability of the circuit
behavior.
3.2.Classicalconditioning
W e now demonstrate a basic application of the STDP behavior in associative learning, as in the classic
example of Pavlov’s dog [ 5]. In figure 9 we show the detailed circuit implementation, where we can see
the spike (pulse) generators in red and green for the ‘meat’ and ‘bell’ for the unconditioned and con-
ditioned stimuli, respectively. The first one has a large intrinsic synaptic efficacy that directly drives the
‘dog’s salivation’ neuron response (blue) with a strong synaptic current (orange). In contrast, the dog’s
response to the bell stimulus is controlled by the STDP conductance GW, which is weak before the learn-
ing. Hence, the corresponding synaptic current (purple) is also small and cannot drive the salivation.
Upon activation of the stimuli pulses, the STDP mechanism will associate the provoked dog’s behav-
ior (blue) to the initially innocuous stimulus (green) that precedes it. The correlated spiking activity
of salivation and bell creates an increase of the synaptic conductance GW, following the STDP mech-
anism described above. When GW efficacy increases enough, the bell stimulus eventually become able
to produce a salivation response. W e say that the dog has learned to associate the sound of the bell to
the food, and now the bell sound drives the dog’s drooling. By the same mechanism, the anti-correlated
stimulation of bell and salivation would lead to the ‘forgetting’ of the previously learned behavior. The
measured data that demonstrate this phenomenon is shown in figure 10, where we observe three phases:
in the first phase, only the innocuous stimulus (bell) is active, shown in green spikes, and fails to pro-
duce a response (salivation) in blue. Then, in the ‘learning’ phase, both stimuli, innocuous and uncon-
ditioned (meat) are active. The former produces the response (salivation), due to the intrinsic strong
synaptic efficacy (orange arrow). The key feature for learning is that the response (salivation) is causally
associated to the innocuous stimulation (bell), i.e. the green spikes shortly precede the blue ones. This
causal correlation produces the increase of the synaptic efficacy (purple arrow) between the green and
blue neurons. As a result, after the associative learning phase, we obtain the ‘conditioned’ behavior,
where the ‘dog’ has learned to respond to the previously innocuous bell stimulus, i.e. the green-neuron
spikes are now provoke themselves the response of the blue neuron.
3.3.Energyrequirements
The quantitative comparison of the energy consumption of our STDP circuit to other analog propos-
als is unfortunately not possible due to the lack a consistent benchmarks and lack of reports. Our STDP
circuit of figure 5 can be separated into three main sub-circuits: the input sub-circuit that keeps traces
of the incoming spikes is comparable to the basic circuit of figure 2, which itself is similar to those of
relevant previous works [ 10–15]. The energy requirement per STDP event of this sub-circuit can be esti-
mated by the cost of producing the traces. They dissipate ∼ CpV2
spike ∼ 10 nF (1 V) 2 ∼ 10 nJ, where we
assumed a typical order of magnitude value for the spike amplitude Vspike. As expected, from the circuit
similarity this estimate is consistent with those that can be obtained from the previous works [ 10–15].
The second sub-circuit is the one denoted as ADC in figure 5. This is comparable to the memristive
integrate-and-fire neuron circuit [ 8], whose energy requirement per STDP event can be estimated as
the cost of producing the train of pulses. Thus, we have ∼ CV2
pnp ∼ 5 nF (5 V) 2 10 ∼ 1250 nJ, where

(digipot), hence, the changes in the synaptic conductance GW.

Figure10. Classic conditioning (associative learning) implemented with the synaptic circuit of figures 5 and 9. Panel (a) shows
spiking traces. The neuron-synapse configuration is shown in panel (b). Initially, neuron green (IN2) that represents the ‘bell’
is excited but not able to drive a ‘dog’s salivation’ response in the output neuron blue (OUT), i.e. they do not have an effective
synaptic coupling. At t = 50 ms an unconditioned stimulus neuron red (IN1) that represents ‘meat’ is activated and drives the
output due to their intrinsic strong synaptic connection (orange arrow). The spikes of the green neuron become causally paired
to those of the blue neuron (i.e green spikes briefly precedes the blue ones). This causal correlation provokes the increase of the
synaptic efficacy between neuron green (pre) and neuron blue (post), which by the STDP mechanism increase their synaptic
coupling (purple arrow). After t = 250 ms of training we observe that the neuron green (bell) is now able to provoke the response
of neuron blue (dog’s salivation).
Vp denotes the amplitude of the pulses and we assumed the number of pulses in the train np = 10. For
concreteness we have adopted the values of the parameters in figures 5 and 6 above. This choice, done
mostly for the sake of illustration, is likely to be overestimating the energy requirement by an order of
magnitude. In fact, the value of Vp could be easily reduced to 3 V and np = 10 is more an upper bound
8
Neuromorph. Comput. Eng.6 (2026) 034015 A d’Hollande et al
than a typical expected value. Nevertheless, our estimate for the second sub-circuit is significantly larger
than that of the first one. This indicates that the ADC sub-circuit is likely to dominate the energy cost
in an actual implementation. The third sub-circuit corresponds to the digipot. Its energy cost in a typi-
cal STDP update can be estimated from its datasheet and the duration of the update from figure 6. W e
estimate for the energy, ∼ 50 µA 5 V 5 ms ∼ 1250 nJ, which is of a similar order of magnitude as that of
the previous sub-circuit.
The apparent high energy cost of the active dendrite sub-circuit can be justified by the improvement
that it provides in the shape of the STDP function ∆GW(∆τ ). In fact, comparing the results from the
basic STDP circuit in figure 2(b) to those of figure 7, we observe that the latter captures much better
the decay of ∆GW with ∆τ and in the biological case [ 2]. The digipot sub-circuit also has a relative
high energy cost. In this case, this can be justified on the merit of simplicity. Hence, this solution may
be useful for the implementation of plastic spiking neural networks with a relatively small number of
neurons, with that number depending on the specific context of the application (e.g brain-machine-
interface, control systems, etc). A digipot based solution may not be appropriate for large scale networks
due to both the energy cost and the large footprint. In fact, this is one of the reasons for the current
ongoing interest in the research of non-volatile memristors [ 16–19].
4.Conclusion
W e have introduced a bio-inspired neuromorphic circuit that implements STDP . Similarly to most previ-
ous implementations our hardware model has input stages where the arrival of the pre- and post- spikes
are detected and respective temporal traces are created. However, a novel distinctive feature of our hard-
ware model is that the detected delay is transformed into a sequence of pulses by and IF stage, which
we call the ADC. This ADC is bio-inspired as it encodes the delay in a train of pulses, which is sent
‘upstream’ to modify the synapse. The number of pulses is inversely related to the delay, realizing the
timing-dependent modulation of the synaptic change, which is a characteristic of STDP that is rarely
captured by hardware models.
Another original feature of our work is that we implement the synaptic with a digipot, which avoids
shortcomings of conventional models using a capacitor and a subthreshold transistor. Moreover, Our
digipot solution has the merits of wide availability, reliability and simple implementation. It therefore
served well our present goal of introducing a novel STDP synaptic circuit model. Nevertheless, as men-
tioned before, if low-energy consumption and small device footprint is a concern, the digipot compo-
nent may eventual be replaced by non-volatile memristors. One further merit of our circuit model is
that such a replacement should be rather straightforward, once the rapidly evolving memristive technol-
ogy becomes mature.
Our hardware model is based on conventional widely available and affordable components, which is
practical for networks of up to few hundreds of synapses. This scale may not be sufficient for complex
artificial intelligence applications. Nevertheless, since it is based on analog hardware, it is well adapted
for applications such as brain-machine-interfaces where the ‘machine’ needs to run in real time and to
incorporate learning plasticity.
While the network scale of our present implementation is relatively modest, there are no a priori
impediments to port the circuit to VLSI CMOS. In fact, all our circuit components are rather standard
for VLSI CMOS, including the current mirrors, teh SR flip-flop (implemented with two NOR gates) and
the digipot. The thyristor of the integrate-and-fire sub-circuit of the ADC has already been ported to
VLSI CMOS in [ 21].
The main appeals of our STDP circuit is its simplicity and bio-inspiration, as it nicely captures the
inverse relation between timing and synaptic change. Moreover, unlike VLSI implementations, our ana-
log electronics approach does not suffer from long design delays nor requires complex fabrication pro-
cedures. It is fully modifiable and all its timescales can be easily tuned, as shown in the present work.
Therefore, it may open a new way to a reliable and practical implementation of learning in intelligent
spiking neural networks.
